Article Summary: Inflation, housing and jobs data to set the tone this week. October CPI and PPI figures in focus. Home sales expected to remain weak. Weekly claims to follow October's job gains. Corporate earnings: CoreWeave, Cisco and SkyDance results due.

Article Title: Berkshire Hathaway's profit falls 28% as Geico struggles: Warren Buffett's insurance giant under focus
Article Text:
Berkshire Hathaway's profit falls 28%

Geico accounts for most of the decline

Noninsurance businesses perform better

Berkshire buys back $9.6 billion in shares

Berkshire Hathaway reported a more than 28% decline in its third-quarter profit, with weaker performance at its insurance businesses and changes in the value of its investments weighing down the results.The conglomerate posted a profit of $22.1 billion, or $15,502 per Class A share, compared with $30.8 billion, or $21,413 per Class A share, in the same quarter last year.The decline was not limited to fluctuations in its investment portfolio.Berkshire's operating earnings, which exclude changes in the value of investments, also fell nearly 6% to $12.7 billion, or $8,907 per Class A share. This was lower than the $13.485 billion, or $9,376.15 per Class A share, reported a year earlier.The four analysts surveyed by FactSet Research had expected operating earnings of $8,821.84 per Class A share.Berkshire has long recommended that investors to focus on operating earnings to understand how its businesses are performing, as changes in investment values can cause significant fluctuations in its overall profit.A major pressure point during the quarter was Berkshire's insurance business. Underwriting profit across its insurers fell to $1.35 billion from $2.37 billion in the corresponding period last year, with Geico accounting for most of the decline.Geico's underwriting profit dropped to $982 million from $1.77 billion a year ago. CFRA Research analyst Cathy Seifert said the insurer was facing a difficult situation as insurance premiums declined while the average cost of claims increased.The company has also been investing more in advertising to attract customers. Investor Chris Ballard, managing director at Check Capital, said he was not disappointed with Geico's numbers, as the spending reflected the company's efforts to bring in more customers. He added that writing new policies more aggressively generally puts pressure on an auto insurer's bottom line.“It should be looking better. Progressive is doing better, but they were doing so well for so long. They had cut their advertising for quite a while there,” said Ballard, whose firm invested in Berkshire. “So we've been kind of expecting this on our end.”The performance of Berkshire's noninsurance operations appeared stronger than that of its insurance business, Seifert said. These businesses have been overseen by Greg Abel for years and include manufacturers such as Precision Castparts, utilities and BNSF railroad.She said these operations appeared to be doing better even though there were no major hurricanes or other catastrophes this year.“I think we’re seeing the businesses that play to Greg’s strengths do well. But the question is what about the rest of the franchise,” Seifert said.Alongside the earnings decline, Berkshire repurchased $9.6 billion worth of its own shares during the third quarter. However, the buybacks likely halted recently after its Class A stock price surged past $878,000, exceeding the level it had reached before Warren Buffett announced his retirement plans at the annual meeting in May 2025.Buffett gave up the chairman's title in September after handing over the chief executive's role to Abel in January.The conglomerate's cash reserves also increased to $377.4 billion at the end of the third quarter, compared with $365.5 billion at the end of June.Berkshire owns several major insurers, including Geico, alongside a collection of large utilities, BNSF railroad and a range of manufacturing and retail businesses, including Precision Castparts and See’s Candy.
Article Summary: Berkshire Hathaway reported a more than 28% decline in its third-quarter profit. The conglomerate posted a profit of $22.1 billion, or $15,502 per Class A share. Underwriting profit across its insurers fell to $1.35 billion from $2.37 billion.

Article Title: Airlines bet on premium travel as rising fuel costs squeeze profits
Article Text:
Airlines turn to premium cabins, upgraded lounges to boost revenue amid fuel costs

Premium travel boosts airline revenues

Premium seat capacity expands

Airlines upgrade airport experience

Airlines are expanding their premium offerings, from luxury seats and Michelin-starred chefs to upgraded airport lounges, as they bet on growing demand for more comfortable and personalised travel experiences.The strategy could further reduce the share of economy-class seats on many flights, with airlines anticipating that as much as 70% of passengers could eventually opt for enhanced seating options or travel in business and first class, according to news agency AFP.The shift comes as airlines contend with significantly higher jet fuel costs linked to the Iran war, making premium services an increasingly important source of revenue.Business-class seats can occupy the floor space of up to four economy seats but may be priced five or six times higher, said Volodymyr Bilotka, a professor at Purdue University specialising in aviation economics."Airlines have traditionally been investing quite a lot into the premium offerings because the profit margins are significantly higher," Bilotka told AFP.American Airlines reported an 18.5% year-on-year increase in premium revenue in its most recent quarter, outperforming the growth in its main cabin revenue by four percentage points."Premium products generate roughly half of the company's ticket revenue on approximately 30 percent of seats today," the airline said.Airlines are also expanding options within economy class, allowing passengers to pay extra for greater comfort and convenience. Customers can now spend as much as $200 for additional legroom or seats near the front of the aircraft, which allow them to disembark earlier.United Airlines announced in July that it would introduce a new Economy Plus option allowing passengers to avoid having someone seated in the middle seat. The service is expected to begin on select flights towards the end of 2026.JetBlue announced BlueFirst, a new first-class service on domestic flights, in September."Customers are increasingly looking for more premium experiences," JetBlue CEO Joanna Geraghty said.The growth in premium travel has also been reflected in airline capacity. The number of premium seats on US flights has increased 33% since 2020, more than twice the growth in mainline seats, according to travel news website Skift.United Airlines said that it had more than doubled its premium-seat capacity between 2015 and 2026 and planned to introduce additional options, including seats offering more elbow room.Delta Air Lines has also invested in its Delta One service, upgrading its food and wine offerings and introducing larger entertainment screens. Its menu includes dishes such as a Wagyu burger.The airline has partnered with Simon Hulstone, chef of a Michelin-starred restaurant in Britain, and award-winning sommelier Andrea Robinson to develop its offerings.The service is planned for new Airbus A350 aircraft, which will have around 150 premium seats and 161 economy seats."Twenty years ago, 90 percent of the seats were main cabin," said Ekrem Dimbiloglu, Delta's managing director for onboard strategy and experience. He added that premium seats could soon account for as much as 70% of capacity on some Delta flights.No major airline has yet introduced a service entirely without economy-class seats. However, British Airways announced in October that the upper deck of its two-tier A380 aircraft would be devoted entirely to premium seating.Consultancy Cirium estimates that premium seats accounted for 19% of the total capacity among 42 airlines belonging to the three major global airline alliances — SkyTeam, Oneworld and Star Alliance — as well as Middle Eastern carriers. The share stood at 17.1% in 2019.The push towards premium travel extends beyond aircraft cabins. Airlines are offering passengers more meal choices before boarding and free Wi-Fi, while investing in new and upgraded airport lounges.Southwest Airlines, which was once known as a discount carrier, is also among the airlines that have announced lounge improvements.The growing focus on passengers willing to pay more for premium amenities could create an opportunity for discount airlines to attract travellers seeking lower fares.However, higher fuel costs have added to the challenges facing the entire aviation industry.
Article Summary: Airlines are expanding their premium offerings, from luxury seats and Michelin- starred chefs to upgraded airport lounges. The shift comes as airlines contend with significantly higher jet fuel costs linked to the Iran war. American Airlines reported an 18.5% year-on-year increase in premium revenue in its most recent quarter.

Article Title: As AI stocks correct, Goldman Sachs sees opportunity in healthcare and non-AI equities
Article Text:
Representative image

Healthcare emerges as potential AI growth area

Goldman Sachs executive outlines market outlook

The US midterm elections could accelerate the ongoing rotation in stock markets, with healthcare emerging as a potential defensive investment amid a correction in artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks, according to Lou Miller, global head of custom basket trading at Goldman Sachs.Speaking on Goldman Sachs' The Markets podcast, Miller said investors had already started moving towards defensive positions ahead of the elections, amid a challenging environment for active investors in the second half of 2026."We've seen people get very defensive. If you look at beta-adjusted net exposure in our prime book, it's definitely at very low levels versus history," he said.Miller pointed to sharp declines in several segments of the AI investment theme. Data centre stocks have fallen 36% from their highs earlier this year, while memory stocks have declined 42%, optical networking stocks 46% and NeoCloud stocks 57%.However, he said the correction had lowered expectations and could leave room for positive surprises."I think the silver lining is the bar is much, much lower for surprises and there are positive catalysts ahead," he said."The multiple for the data centre trade is about half of what it was in June," Miller added, saying valuations had moved to healthier levels.Miller identified healthcare as a possible beneficiary of the next phase of AI adoption, saying the sector could be among the few to see accelerating earnings growth next year."I think the next leg of the AI trade is actually healthcare, and I think that's also a very defensive sector that historically is very uncorrelated to AI," he said.He noted that healthcare companies were increasingly adopting AI in areas such as medical tools and diagnostics, with the sector moving from challenges towards growth opportunities.Miller, however, cautioned against treating traditional defensive sectors such as consumer staples as automatically attractive, arguing that elevated valuations had reduced their appeal."Expensive defensives I don't think are defensive," he said.He suggested investors focus on companies with strong balance sheets, quality earnings and healthy free cash flows.Outlining his preferred investment strategy, Miller said: "I think the S&P 500 excluding AI is the trade."He cited attractive valuations and earnings growth prospects as reasons for his preference.Looking ahead, Miller identified employment, inflation, corporate earnings and the US Federal Reserve's December 9 policy decision as key factors that could influence markets.On the outlook for US stocks towards the end of the year, he expressed cautious optimism, anticipating a modest rally that he described as a "relaxed Santa Rally".
Article Summary: US midterm elections could accelerate the ongoing rotation in stock markets. Lou Miller, global head of custom basket trading at Goldman Sachs, identified healthcare as a potential beneficiary of the next phase of AI adoption. Miller said investors had already started moving towards defensive positions ahead of the elections.

Article Title: Elon Musk's futuristic dream vehicle to cease production - What went wrong with Tesla's Cybertruck
Article Text:
Why is Elon Musk pulling the plug on Tesla's Cybertruck

1. Sales and pricing failed to meet expectations

2. Its design made it impossible to ignore

3. Musk's political image became a problem for some customers

Tesla's Cybertruck arrived with big ambitions, a futuristic design and Elon Musk 's backing.Now, it is bidding adieu.The high-tech pickup was meant to shake up the automobile industry, but its journey is coming to an end. Musk announced on Friday that Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production around the middle of 2027 at its facility outside Austin, Texas.The move will make room for increased production of the company's Cybercab robotaxi, as Tesla shifts its focus towards autonomous vehicles.But what led to the Cybertruck's early exit? A combination of disappointing sales, a price tag that was much higher than initially promised and growing controversy surrounding Musk.Musk had projected annual production of 250,000 Cybertrucks, but sales remained far below that target. Kelley Blue Book estimated that Tesla sold just 20,237 units last year, around half the previous year's sales. Sales through September this year fell another 28%. Spencer Penn, a former Tesla executive who left before the Cybertruck's launch and now heads software developer LightSource, said electric trucks had struggled to attract demand.“A really controversial vehicle unveiled by a controversial individual into a market where none of the electric trucks have been able to really capture demand,” he said.Pricing was another hurdle. Musk had promised a price tag below $40,000, but the first Cybertrucks sold for double that amount or more. Penn, who had booked a pre-sale reservation, eventually decided against buying one after the promised price failed to materialise.With its sharp angles and stainless-steel body, the Cybertruck looked more like a science-fiction vehicle than a conventional pickup. Its 2019 unveiling grabbed attention when a Tesla designer threw a metal ball at its supposedly unbreakable glass, only for the window to shatter. A second attempt on another window ended the same way. Musk, however, remained convinced about his vision.“I just wanted to make a futuristic battle tank — something that looks like it could come out of ‘Blade Runner’ or ‘Aliens’ or something like that but was also highly functional,” he told Automotive News.He called it “a better sports car than a Porsche 911” and “a better truck than an F-150.” The design drew both admiration and ridicule. Armen Hareyan, whose Torque News site covers autos, said: “Few vehicles in history have generated as much attention. The Cybertruck became a cultural symbol – loved, mocked and impossible to ignore.”Penn initially found its appearance revolting and called it “madness”, but his opinion changed the more he looked at it. He eventually saw it as an example of Tesla's adventurous spirit and willingness to take risks. “Some of these bets work and some of these bets don’t,” he said.Musk's association with several right-wing figures, particularly US President Donald Trump, alienated some Tesla customers. As his image shifted from an eccentric innovator to a polarising figure trading his billions for political influence, some previously passionate owners rushed to sell their cars. Others put stickers on their bumpers reading, “I bought this before Elon went crazy.”The backlash extended to demonstrations outside Tesla showrooms, with organisers also urging investors to sell their shares. Some protests turned violent, with Molotov cocktails thrown at Tesla vehicles, charging stations set ablaze and dealerships covered in graffiti. Cybertruck owners faced hostility too, with some being shouted at with “Nazi!” and receiving extended middle fingers.Ross Blankenship, a Cybertruck owner, said that he disliked seeing a vehicle he loved turned into a political symbol. Its futuristic appearance had reminded him of “Halo”, the science-fiction video game he played as a child.“I had that sort of child in me wanting to be part of something cool that would change the future of automotive,” Blankenship said in a call from his Cybertruck as he drove through Sunnyside, Colorado.Although he said he agreed with Musk on politics, he was unhappy about the vehicle becoming associated with the controversy.“I never bought it for any other reason than the fascination with the future technology of trucks … so that was a little heartbreaking.” The Cybertruck's discontinuation also comes as Tesla shifts its attention towards autonomous vehicles. Musk said winding down production would allow the company to make more Cybercab robotaxis, a segment on which he is betting Tesla's future.For a vehicle that Musk once called Tesla's best product, the planned shutdown marks an unceremonious end to a much-hyped project. Yet, it has not lost all its fans. Blankenship said he would buy another Cybertruck again in a heartbeat. He called the end of its production “a sad moment.”
Article Summary: Elon Musk announced on Friday that Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production around the middle of 2027 at its facility outside Austin, Texas. The move will make room for increased production of the company's Cybercab robotaxi, as Tesla shifts its focus towards autonomous vehicles.

Article Title: Why new LNG projects may not prevent a global gas crunch this winter
Article Text:
Representative image

New LNG projects unlikely to offset Persian Gulf losses

IEA outlines two scenarios for winter gas supplies

Global natural gas supplies could tighten further during the 2026–27 winter heating season as disruptions to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz continue to affect the global liquefied natural gas (LNG) market, the International Energy Agency (IEA) has warned.In its report, the IEA described the disruption as an unprecedented supply shock, noting that LNG loadings from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates declined by 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) year-on-year between March and October 2026.This contributed to a 5 per cent, or 20 bcm, fall in global LNG output, as additional supplies from new projects only partly offset reduced deliveries from the Persian Gulf, according to news agency ANI.With transit through the Strait of Hormuz remaining severely restricted in late October, the agency warned that the disruption could continue to weigh on global gas supplies during the winter months."The disruption of LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz creates unprecedented uncertainty for the global LNG market ahead of the 2026/27 winter," the report said.It added that "the supply shock looks set to keep imposing tighter market conditions during the northern hemisphere winter, even as supply from new liquefaction plants around the globe continues to grow."Depending on how quickly LNG shipments through the Strait of Hormuz recover, global LNG supply could decline by 10–25 bcm year-on-year between November and March, the IEA said.The scope for increasing pipeline gas supplies remains limited, as long-distance pipelines generally operate close to their designed capacity. This restricts their ability to compensate for shortages in LNG deliveries.North American exporters are expected to drive LNG supply growth during the winter, supported by expanding projects in the United States, Canada and Mexico. Additional volumes are also expected from new facilities in West Africa and Australia.The IEA projects that new LNG projects will add around 18 bcm of supply during the winter, while existing facilities could contribute another 3 bcm. This would take total incremental supply from outside the Persian Gulf to slightly over 20 bcm.However, the additional volumes are not expected to make up for the shortfall from Qatar and the UAE."In total, new and legacy projects outside the Persian Gulf could contribute slightly over 20 bcm of incremental supply y-o-y in the winter period. Despite the strong growth, this extra supply would remain insufficient to compensate for the lost volumes from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates," the report said.The agency outlined two possible scenarios depending on when the Strait of Hormuz resumes normal operations.If the waterway begins progressively reopening in January 2027, global LNG supply could decline by around 9 bcm, or 3 per cent, year-on-year during the winter period.However, if the Strait remains closed until the end of March 2027, the decline could be sharper, with global LNG supply falling by around 20 bcm, or 7 per cent, year-on-year.The IEA also cautioned that unplanned outages and delays in ramping up production at new LNG projects could create additional downside risks to global supplies, particularly while the disruption in the Middle East continues.
Article Summary: Disruption to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz continues to affect the global liquefied natural gas market. LNG loadings from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates declined by 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) year-on-year between March and October 2026.

Article Title: US stocks: Wall street bounces back in green after hitting 18-month low as chipmakers rally
Article Text:
Wall Street bounces back after days of decline

Chipmakers lead Wall Street's recovery

Texas data centre plans add to AI regulation concerns

Asian and European markets extend losses

Wall Street rebounded from its 18-month low on Friday, led by a sharp recovery in semiconductor stocks, as investors assessed the potential impact of Democratic election victories on the US artificial intelligence (AI) industry.The recovery followed a steep selloff in the previous session, triggered by fears that the election results could lead to tighter regulations for the AI sector, wiping out trillions of dollars in global stock market value. The gains were led by technology, communication services and industrial stocks.The S&P 500 rose a marginal 0.31% and the Nasdaq Composite advanced 1.1%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.46%.However, despite Friday's recovery, all three indices ended the week lower following the previous session's sharp losses.Semiconductor stocks emerged as the biggest beneficiaries of Friday's rebound. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index gained 4.2%, recovering after suffering its biggest single-day decline since April 2025.Nvidia shares climbed nearly 3%, reversing some of the losses from its previous session, when the stock recorded its worst performance since January 2025.At the time, the emergence of Chinese AI model DeepSeek, which offered a low-cost alternative, had triggered a sharp market reaction.The recovery extended across other major chipmakers. AMD, Intel and Micron Technology ended the session between 5% and 11% higher. Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX also bounced back, gaining 4% and nearly 9%, respectively, after declining earlier in the week.Despite Friday's gains, uncertainty over the future regulatory environment continued to weigh on investor sentiment."Most of the disruption of the AI buildout will not probably occur but it's just the uncertainty of the change in government from Republican-led to Democratic-led, not only at the federal level but the state, local levels," said Gerry Sparrow, president and portfolio manager at Sparrow Capital Management."That's causing some disruption in the expectations of investors ... The volatility around elections or any political event, whether it be war or terrorist attack, is always going to disrupt the market."The prospect of tighter oversight of the AI industry is also emerging at the state level. Texas Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said on Thursday that the state would introduce new laws to protect local communities from further large-scale data centre development.Texas already has a substantial share of data centres in the US, making the proposed measures an additional concern for investors tracking the expansion of AI infrastructure.The latest uncertainty comes as the AI trade is already facing questions over the enormous costs involved in building data centres and other infrastructure. Investors are concerned that the scale of these investments could limit future returns.These worries have added to market volatility, triggering margin calls and unsettling retail investors as well as hedge funds.Friday's recovery on Wall Street was in sharp contrast with the performance of other major global markets, where the selloff continued.European equities weakened, with the STOXX 600 declining 1%. In Asia, Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's KOSPI both plunged around 6%.The Nikkei recorded its biggest one-day decline since US President Donald Trump's "Liberation Day" trade tariff turmoil in April 2025. The fall was comparable to Wall Street's previous session, when US stocks suffered their biggest single-day decline since the same period.The broader global market indicators also remained under pressure. The MSCI All-World index fell 0.68%, while MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan dropped nearly 3%.
Article Summary: Semiconductor stocks emerged as the biggest beneficiaries of Friday's rebound. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index gained 4.2%, recovering after suffering its biggest single-day decline since April 2025. Despite Friday's recovery, all three indices ended the week lower following the previous session's sharp losses.

Article Title: US-China agree to continue trade talks as Washington presses Beijing to fulfil Busan deal commitments
Article Text:
US-China agree to keep trade talks going

China and the US have agreed to continue consultations to ensure stable and positive trade relations, local media Xinhua reported.The development comes as Washington pushes Beijing to fulfil the commitments made under the trade truce agreed between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Busan last year.The US has raised concerns that China is falling short of its promises on rare earth supplies, critical minerals and agricultural purchases.These concerns were discussed during a phone call on Friday morning between US treasury secretary Scott Bessent, US trade representative Jamieson Greer and Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng, who oversees trade negotiations with Washington.During the call, the US officials told China that it needed to fully deliver on the commitments made under the Busan agreement. In a post on X on Friday, he said, “ Today, US trade representative Greer and I spoke with Vice Premier He Lifeng about the US-China economic relationship and implementation of the Busan arrangement.Bessent further raised concerns about China's recent actions. "I emphasized the importance of China fully and immediately honoring its commitments, raised concerns about recent Chinese actions and underscored that progress depends on concrete results.”One of Washington's biggest concerns is China's supply of rare earths. US officials told the FT in September that China was meeting only about two-thirds of its commitments on rare earths under the Busan agreement.A person familiar with the matter said Beijing had not increased supplies even after Bessent raised the issue directly with He in New York in September, ahead of Xi's meeting with Trump in Washington.China has rejected the US claims that it is not meeting its promises on rare earth supplies.The two countries also differ over agricultural purchases. The US believes China has met its commitment to buy soyabeans but has not fulfilled its promises on other agricultural products.Washington is also concerned about China's restrictions on exports of yttrium to Japan. The rare earth is used in products ranging from jet engines to missiles. Japan makes components for products manufactured in the US, and Japanese companies have warned their government that their stockpiles of yttrium are running dangerously low.The Busan trade truce was agreed in October 2025 and was originally due to expire on January 10. However, during Xi's visit to Washington in September, the two countries extended the deadline by two months, until January 2027, after negotiators failed to resolve their differences.
Article Summary: US-China agree to keep trade talks going to ensure stable and positive trade relations. Washington pushes Beijing to fulfil commitments made under the trade truce agreed between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Busan last year. The US has raised concerns that China is falling short of its promises on rare earth supplies, critical minerals and agricultural purchases.

Article Title: Pakistan's external debt nearly doubles to $135 billion in 10 years, China biggest lender
Article Text:
Pakistan's external debt doubles

Pakistan's external borrowing has nearly doubled in the last 10 years, reaching $135.1 billion in 2025, with China accounting for the largest share of the country's outstanding debt among individual creditors.The increase comes as borrowing by developing economies also accelerated, taking the external debt of low- and middle-income countries to a record $9.4 trillion, according to the World Bank's International Debt Report 2026.Pakistan's external debt stood at $68.673 billion in 2015 before rising to $135.107 billion in 2025, Dawn reported, citing the World Bank report.Public and publicly guaranteed borrowing made up the bulk of the debt at $107.076 billion. This was followed by private non-guaranteed debt of $17.58 billion and short-term debt of $10.45 billion.A breakdown of the public and publicly guaranteed component shows that multilateral institutions accounted for $56.83 billion, while bilateral creditors were owed $42.43 billion. Private creditors held claims worth another $7.8 billion.Among individual lenders, China had the highest outstanding exposure to Pakistan at $22.4 billion.The World Bank followed with $19.2 billion, while the Asian Development Bank (ADB) accounted for $16.83 billion.The terms of borrowing also varied considerably depending on the source of credit. Pakistan's loans from official creditors had an average maturity of 16 years and included a four-year grace period. The average interest rate on these loans was 3.6 per cent.Private borrowing was considerably more expensive, carrying an average interest rate of 8.6 per cent. These loans had a three-year repayment period and a one-year grace period.Pakistan also received financial support from key lenders during 2025. China extended the maturities on $2 billion of its loans, while the International Monetary Fund (IMF) made $2.3 billion in fresh disbursements under the Extended Fund Facility and Resilience and Sustainability Facility arrangements. These arrangements were aimed at supporting Pakistan's long-term economic stability.The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (Menap) region recorded improvements in its debt-service and interest ratios. However, its external debt-to-gross national income (GNI) ratio moved in the opposite direction, increasing from 26.7 per cent to 29.4 per cent in 2025.This was the biggest single-year increase in the ratio among all regions, reflecting continued accumulation of external debt.Pakistan's rising debt was part of a wider increase in external borrowing across low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Their combined external debt grew 5.5 per cent to $9.4 trillion in 2025, marking the sharpest increase in four years.The expansion was supported by a recovery in bond issuances, a weaker US dollar and renewed interest among private investors in lending to developing economies. This also marked a forceful return of private creditors to these markets.However, access to capital markets came with higher costs, particularly for the poorest countries, which faced some of the highest borrowing costs in decades.Debt-service payments across these economies continued to climb for the fifth year in a row. At the same time, stronger economic growth helped stabilise some debt ratios, while net long-term debt transfers turned positive after several years of outflows.The increase in borrowing was more pronounced among countries eligible for International Development Association (IDA) financing. Their external debt rose 8.1 per cent to $1.3 trillion.Low-income countries recorded an even sharper increase, with external debt climbing 8.9 per cent to $262.4 billion in 2025. This was their biggest increase since 2020.
Article Summary: Pakistan's external debt stood at $68.673 billion in 2015 before rising to $135.107 billion in 2025. Public and publicly guaranteed borrowing made up the bulk of the debt at $107.076 billion. China had the highest outstanding exposure to Pakistan at $22.4 billion.

Article Title: 1.14 lakh startups generate more than 12 lakh jobs in India: Finance ministry
Article Text:
Finance Ministry

NEW DELHI: More than 1.14 lakh startups in India have created over 12 lakh jobs so far, the finance ministry said in its latest review of the Indian economy.In the report titled, ‘The Indian Economy: A Review January 2024’, the Department of Economic Affairs said that the 1.14 lakh startups recognised by the government under the 'Startup India initiative’ created more than 12 lakh jobs (as of October 2023).The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023, the document read.Despite facing global challenges in 2023 like valuation issues, few IPOs, regulatory changes and macroeconomic and geopolitical trends, India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year.The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion (from 2019 to 2023), according to a recent report by Nasscom in collaboration with Zinnov.“In 2023, despite facing global economic and regulatory challenges, Indian tech startups have prioritised the imperative of enhancing their business fundamentals, driving profitability and growth,” said Debjani Ghosh, President, Nasscom.“The proliferation of tech startups in tier 2 and 3 cities marks the ecosystem's resilience,” she added.Navigating 2024, tech startup founders expect to continue the revenue growth path with measured steps focusing on optimising expenditure and maximising profitability for B2B tech startups.Investments in deeptech will continue an upward trend in 2024. With generative AI (GenAI) acceleration, 70 per cent of start-up founders are embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in their solutions.As funding becomes scarce for the Indian startup ecosystem in general, the explosion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has given a new lease of life to entrepreneurs and founders in the country, as the Centre extends support to the sector.
Article Summary: The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023. India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year. The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion.

Article Title: Startups Revolutionizing Carbon Dioxide into Valuable Products
Article Text: For most perfume makers, ingredients to make it smell great are the most important feature. But for Stafford Sheehan, a cofounder and chemist at Air Company, the most important part of perfume-making has no scent at all.New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. While the pale yellow-color Air Eau de Parfum is about 50% more expensive than Coco Chanel’s signature No. 5, Sheehan says his product is uniquely valuable: Every 50-milliliter bottle uses 3.6 grams of CO2 that otherwise would have been released into the atmosphere. Its package reads: “Turning CO2 into something beautiful.”While the volume of CO2 utilized in the bottle is extremely small, Air Company’s perfume showcases one way the coming wave of captured carbon can be put to use. Renewable energy and electric cars alone won’t be enough to cut CO2 emissions to zero. The world will almost certainly need to capture billions of tons of the gas annually in the coming decades. Large amounts will likely be stored underground.Using it — so-called carbon capture and utilization, or CCU — to create new products from perfume to jet fuel could be an important tool in the fight against climate change, too, though the nascent industry has major hurdles to overcome.Roughly 230 million tons of CO2 are utilized every year, according to a 2019 report by the International Energy Agency. While roughly one-third of that is reused to force more oil from the ground — hardly a carbon-neutral process — CCU advocates say that the number of companies coming up with new uses for carbon has mushroomed in recent years, paving a way to unlock climate benefits. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology and lower costs.Calgary-based CleanO2 transforms CO2 captured from building heating boilers into feedstock to make soap. Newlight Technologies, a biotechnology startup based in California, takes carbon pulled directly from the air and turns it into biodegradable plastics. Germany’s Covestro AG, one of the world’s largest polymer manufacturers, is also switching some of its fossil fuel-based feedstocks to carbon-derived materials for everything ranging from car shells to medical devices and stadium roofs.Most companies working on CO2-sequestering products are still in their infancy. To grow the emerging sector, global venture capitalists in 2022 poured nearly $500 million into carbon utilization businesses, according to the IEA. That’s in stark contrast to 2015, when barely any venture money went to technologies that utilize CO2.“It’s just a whole different landscape today than it was a decade ago,” says Sasha Mackler, executive director of the energy program at Washington, DC-based non-profit Bipartisan Policy Center.Jennifer Holmgren, chief executive officer of LanzaTech Global Inc., has experienced the shifting sentiment firsthand. The Illinois-based company uses a carbon-eating bacteria – discovered in the guts of rabbits and preserved as powder – to make alternative ethanol in bioreactors not dissimilar to how breweries ferment beer. In the early 2010s, when Holmgren touted carbon-derived ethanol to prospective customers, her sales pitch was met with skepticism.But the tide began turning later that decade. In 2018, the company’s jet fuel produced from the emissions of a Chinese steel mill helped power a Transatlantic flight. LanzaTech has also inked agreements with airlines including Japan’s All Nippon Airways to supply CO2-derived jet fuel. And LanzaJet, the company’s spin-off, plans to start producing sustainable jet fuels at a commercial scale this year.Yet for all the hype around sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) using captured carbon, the industry is still an extremely small player. Almost every major airline in the world has pledged to use at least 10% sustainable jet fuels by 2030, yet SAF makes up only 0.1% of global aviation fuel supply — and much of it is made from sources other than captured CO2, such as used cooking oil.“There’s a lot more interest because consumers have become much more interested in buying things that are lower carbon,” says Holmgren. That’s enabled LanzaTech to expand the number of products that utilize CO2.American plastic container maker Plastipak, for instance, has partnered with LanzaTech to produce carbon-derived packaging materials, while polyester converted from LanzaTech’s ethanol has replaced its petroleum-based counterpart at a pilot scale in Lululemon shorts, Zara dresses, H&M yoga pants, On running shoes and Craghoppers jackets. Like SAF, though, there’s still a long way to go for CO2-derived polyester to reach meaningful levels of use.Momentum to grow beyond one-off products and low-scale production has also been supercharged by a growing array of regulations and incentives around the world. For instance, the Inflation Reduction Act that US President Joe Biden signed in 2022 raised the tax credit for carbon capture and utilization by more than 70% to $60 per metric ton in an effort to make costly projects more financially appealing.To keep the climate within habitable limits, the IEA estimates that carbon capture will have to grow to 7.6 billion tons of CO2 annually by mid-century. CCU will play a role, though just how big remains to be seen. Not every use case is created equal and some approaches, such as dissolving compressed CO2 in water to make carbonated beverages, only store the gas temporarily. To quantify the true climate benefit of carbon utilization, experts say third-party verification is badly needed.The rise of CCU technology comes as another key approach in President Biden’s net-zero roadmap is hitting a bit of a wall. Carbon capture and storage — that is, gathering CO2 as it’s released from a coal-fired power plant or other emissions source and sequestering it underground — has faced challenges because carbon is often captured in one place and stored in another. That requires pipelines to transport the gas, which many local communities have opposed. Blackrock-backed Navigator, for example, recently announced it was scrapping a planned 1,300-mile CO2 pipeline.Carbon utilization companies say that they can sidestep that issue by using carbon near or at where it’s captured.At its 12-acre factory in Brooklyn, Glenwood Mason Supply demonstrates how. The concrete manufacturer takes CO2 captured at a residential building by its partner company, CarbonQuest, and uses a technique licensed from low-carbon concrete startup CarbonCure to convert the compressed carbon into a powder not unlike dry ice. It then injects it into industrial mixers. There, the CO2 meets cement, sand and aggregate, setting off a series of chemical reactions. The final result is concrete blocks with CO2 sealed in.The technique not only stores carbon but it can also make the blocks marginally stronger. The company estimates that it has utilized about 100 tons of CO2 in total since 2020. Even if the blocks break down, the stored carbon won’t be released as CO2 because it’s been mineralized.“Cement is a big offender in carbon emissions,” says Constance Cincotta, founder of the concrete factory. She became intrigued by the technology and its ability to lower her company's climate impact after hearing about it at an industry conference in the early 2010s. But it wasn't until CarbonCure came on the scene a few years ago that the prospect of CO2-storing cement became tangible. Glenwood Mason then sourced CO2 locally from CarbonQuest, which captures carbon from buildings in New York. Those factors have enabled large-scale production.While Cincotta’s intended to help the planet, she and her team discovered that sinking CO2 into concrete blocks is good for the business, too. In 2019, New York City — where the majority of the company’s concrete blocks are sold — passed a regulation requiring all buildings to shrink their carbon footprint 40% by the end of the decade. Glenwood Mason’s phones have been ringing ever since, with calls from architects and property developers who want to leverage their lower-carbon building materials to cut emissions, says Jeff Hansen, the company’s vice president in architectural sales and marketing.The factory’s CO2-storing concrete blocks also caught the eye of Amazon.com Inc, which in 2022 persuaded a real estate developer to purchase roughly 50,000 blocks for the construction of a new warehouse in New York that Amazon has leased. Had Glenwood Mason not sealed CO2 in its blocks, it wouldn’t have won the contract, Hansen says. To figure out how to pack more carbon into its products, the company has set up a laboratory in its factory to test the reaction between CO2 and other concrete feedstocks under different temperatures and humidity levels.But figuring out the right formula is only one consideration. Utilizing CO2 often comes with an additional cost. As the demand for CO2-derived products climbs, that green premium is expected to go down. Yet “it’s very hard to be a cost parity with a 100-year-old industry that doesn’t even have to pay for its externalities,” says Holmgren of LanzaTech. Even with economies of scale, Holmgren estimates that carbon-containing fabrics will still likely cost as much as 20% higher than conventional ones.“It’s unlikely that we will ever be a cost parity,” she says.In addition to the cost barrier, CCU companies also have to convince end users that may be suspicious of unproven new technologies.Changing feedstocks “does come with risks,” says Keith Wiggins, chief executive officer of Econic Technologies, a British startup that specializes in making carbon-derived chemicals. To get risk-averse industries onboard, Wiggins says his company is laser-focused on those that are under consumer pressure to change course.That strategy seems to be working. Econic has teamed up with three manufacturers in the US, China and India to produce mattresses, outdoor garments and building insulation materials that utilize CO2. The first batch of products using the company’s technology are scheduled to enter the market in 2024.For all the promise of the carbon utilization industry, it remains to be seen if it can challenge the status quo. While Air Company started selling carbon-derived perfume in 2021, the startup has yet to build its first commercial plant, Sheehan says, citing the time-consuming process needed for collecting data and fine-tuning the technology for large-scale production.Fow now, the company’s demonstration facility in New York City — where CO2 and hydrogen gas flow through tubes into a reactor to form chemical reactions, aided by catalysts made from a confidential mixture of metals — is designed to yield at least 10,000 gallons of CO2-derived liquid annually. The limited production capacity has left many orders for its perfume — as well as jet fuels and Air Vodka, another popular product made from CO2 — unfilled.“We need to scale these facilities to the size of oil refineries today in order to have the impact on climate change that we want to have,” Sheehan says.
Article Summary: New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology.

Article Title: E-commerce firm Udaan raises $340 million ahead of planned IPO
Article Text: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain and boost vendor partnerships ahead of a stock market debut planned for 2025.The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt, the Bangalore-based company said in a statement Thursday. The round was led by M&G Plc and existing investors including Lightspeed Venture Partners and DST Global participated.The round “fully funds our business plan,” Vaibhav Gupta, Udaan co-founder and chief executive officer, said in the statement. “It enables our continued journey of growth and profitability, positioning us well to be public-market ready in the next 12-18 months.”Udaan, which competes with Reliance Industries Ltd. and Walmart Inc.’s Flipkart in helping smaller merchants source their goods, runs an online marketplace and logistics networks that help mum-and-pop stores get quicker deliveries and cut traditional middlemen out. That kind of digital-led wholesale business, though a very small part of India’s overall retail market, is expected to swell to $150 billion in sales in a decade, according to McKinsey & Co.The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas, Gupta told Bloomberg News last month.Udaan was founded in 2016 by three engineers who previously worked at Flipkart. The trio together ran the company until Gupta, one of the founders, took over as CEO in 2021. The other two founders — Amod Malviya and Sujeet Kumar — are board members.
Article Summary: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain. The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt. The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas.

Article Title: Minuscule AI startup raises $41 million to tap India growth
Article Text: A generative artificial intelligence startup targeting the Indian market raised $41 million in fresh funding, the largest such round by an early-stage AI contender in the country.Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages at price points that the country’s 1.4 billion people can afford. The Series A funding round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, and participants included Silicon Valley billionaire Vinod Khosla’s Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners, formerly Sequoia Capital India & Southeast Asia, Sarvam said Thursday.The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co-founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems as well as tools for creating apps for the meager compute infrastructure available to developers in India. The startup has a total of 18 employees and is just opening an office in the city."What we are showing is that you can build large language models with limited resources,” Raghavan said in a phone interview. "We are building at a smaller scale and demonstrating that these can be extremely cost and energy efficient so they can be accessed by everyone."Large language models, like OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama, are powerful AI systems that understand by learning from vast amounts of diverse data from the internet and elsewhere to summarize, translate, and create text, audio and video for a wide range of applications. The rivalry to develop ever-more sophisticated models is heating up in Silicon Valley and such efforts have attracted billions of dollars in investments.
Article Summary: Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages. The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co- founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems.

Article Title: ZestMoney set to shut operations this month
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Buy now Pay Later (BNPL) startup ZestMoney has decided to shut operations. The move will impact some 150 employees of the firm, the company's management told employees in a town hall on Tuesday. ZestMoney did not comment. It is learnt that the firm will shut down by the end of this month.The move comes after attempts by the Bengaluru-based startup to get acquired by larger peer PhonePe failed. The deal was called off earlier this year after a due diligence process undertaken by PhonePe, while evaluating the potential acquisition failed to meet its bar. The Walmart-owned fintech major had, however, hired some 130 of ZestMoney's employees.
Article Summary: The move will impact some 150 employees of the firm, the company's management told employees in a town hall on Tuesday. The move comes after attempts by the Bengaluru-based startup to get acquired by larger peer PhonePe failed. The Walmart-owned fintech major had, however, hired some 130 of ZestMoney's employees.

Article Title: Startups will play important role in helping India become 3rd largest economy: CEA Nageswaran
Article Text:
Chief Economic Advisor V Anantha Nageswaran





THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: Startups will play an important role in helping India become the third largest economy in the world, Chief Economic Advisor (CEA) to the Union government V Anantha Nageswaran has said.Nageswaran said that tier-2 and 3 cities, including Kerala's capital, have become game-changers in helping startups flourish in the country due to improvements in infrastructure and supportive policies of the government, according to a KSUM release.The CEA, during his Leadership Talk on the concluding day of the Huddle Global 2023 organised by the Kerala Startup Mission (KSUM), said that India was the fifth largest economy on course to become the third largest in a few years."In fact, I will say 7-in-7 is the buzz slogan, that is 7 trillion USD economy in seven years. Seven trillion USD economy size by 2030 is possible if India maintains its present growth trajectory, and in that journey startup entrepreneurs are going to play an important role," he is quoted as having said in the release.He was of the view that the active participation of startups in India in developing business models on the foundation of expanding physical and digital infrastructure will continue to generate efficiency, revenue and economic returns for the country."The last decade has seen an exceptional transformation in the startup landscape in India, which has emerged as the third largest ecosystem globally, with over 1.12 lakh startups presently recognised by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) across 763 districts."Among them, more than 110 are unicorns with a total valuation of around USD 350 billion," he said.The CEA further said that the country ranks second in innovation quality.He said that innovation in India was not just limited to certain sectors as startups were solving problems in 56 industrial sectors, with 13 per cent of them from IT services, nine per cent from health and life sciences, seven per cent from education, five per cent from agriculture and five per cent from food and beverages.Nageswaran also said it was significant that 49 per cent of the startups were from tier-2 and 3 cities which have turned to be game-changers as the business advantages in these locations enable entrepreneurs to operate at lower costs as compared to tier-1 cities."Apart from improved infrastructure and the government's pro-active policies, the availability of a technically skilled talent pool is a huge advantage for startups to set up and flourish in tier-2 and tier-3 cities," he said.He said that historically there was a perception that small towns were difficult places to conduct business."...but with improved internet penetration, vastly better physical infrastructure, road, rail and air connectivity and supportive government policies, this is no longer true," he said.He also noted Kerala's startup journey has been an inspiring one.The CEA said that KSUM has served as the catalyst since its establishment in 2006 to promote change that propelled the state into the forefront of the global startup arena.KSUM is the Kerala government's nodal agency established in 2006 for entrepreneurship development and incubation activities in the state.Nageswaran said that with over 4,000 registered tech startups, 63 incubators and 10 lakh square feet of incubation space, KSUM has not only met its goal of promoting technology-based entrepreneurship but has also earned the distinguished position of being among the world's top business incubators.The November 16-18 fifth edition of Huddle Global, India's biggest beachside startup conclave, was organised by KSUM at Adimalathura beach, near Vizhinjam, here.Attended by around 1,500 delegates, the event displayed sophisticated products from emerging sectors such as robotics, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Augmented Reality, Virtual Reality, life sciences, space tech, blockchain, IoT, e-governance, fintech, healthtech, agritech, edutech and SaaS from across the country.
Article Summary: Chief Economic Advisor V Anantha Nageswaran said tier-2 and 3 cities, including Kerala's capital, have become game-changers in helping startups flourish in the country. CEA said that India was the fifth largest economy on course to become the third largest in a few years.

Article Title: E-Commerce startup Udaan to trim costs ahead of 2025 IPO
Article Text: E-commerce startup Udaan is working to curb costs and forge new partnerships with consumer brands in India as it prepares to go public in 2025.Udaan, which competes with Reliance Industries Ltd. and Walmart Inc.’s Flipkart in helping smaller merchants source their goods, will make an operating profit within 18 months, Chief Executive Officer Vaibhav Gupta said in an interview. That’s set to happen around the same time as its initial public offering, he said.The priority “is steady and predictable financial performance,” Gupta said. “Second, strategically we want to ensure that we are top of mind with shopkeepers, with big manufacturers, and we maintain our relative market share.”Lightspeed Venture Partners-backed Udaan is among startups trying to tap the rapid growth of India’s economy and consumer market, while meeting investor demands for profitability. Udaan, which at its peak employed thousands, joined fellow Indian startups in slashing jobs last year and tightening internal controls and compliance. It now has about 1,800 staff, and Gupta didn’t specify if further job cuts are needed.Corporate governance lapses at Indian online tutoring firm Byju’s, once the country’s top startup with a valuation of $22 billion, shone a light at unique challenges faced by founders in the South Asian nation and drove companies to be more diligent.“We continue to move towards more professionalized management, professionalized board and also institutionalized shareholders as we go towards public markets,” Gupta said.Udaan is yet to decide whether it will list in India or overseas. It was valued at more than $3 billion in a 2021 funding round, and was in talks to raise $400 million, Business Standard reported in September. Lightspeed owns about 35% of Udaan, while Tencent Holdings Ltd. holds 6%.The company was founded in 2016 by three engineers who previously worked at Flipkart. The trio together ran Udaan until Gupta, one of the founders, took over as CEO in 2021. The other two founders — Amod Malviya and Sujeet Kumar — are board members.Udaan built an online marketplace and logistics networks that help mum-and-pop stores get quicker deliveries and cut traditional middlemen out. That kind of digital-led wholesale business still accounts for a very small part of India’s overall retail market but can balloon to $150 billion in sales and yield a 100% return on capital invested in a decade, according to McKinsey & Co. estimates published in the Mint newspaper.Bengaluru-based Udaan has also ventured into financing through its fintech unit which helps shopkeepers get working capital loans to buy inventory. That business is profitable before taxes and is growing 70% annually, Gupta said.“That’s a second business in the overall umbrella of Udaan trying to organize trade in the country,” Gupta said. “In addition to commerce, financing becomes an important market opportunity.”
Article Summary: Udaan will make an operating profit within 18 months, Chief Executive Officer Vaibhav Gupta says. Udaan competes with Reliance Industries Ltd. and Walmart Inc.’s Flipkart in helping smaller merchants source their goods. The priority “is steady and predictable financial performance,” Gupta said.

Article Title: Kerala-based startup bags prestigious awards
Article Text: KOCHI: A company under the Kerala Startup Mission (KSUM), which primarily connects devotees with temples through a cost-free Customer Relationship Management Solution (CRM), has bagged two prestigious awards in a week's time, boosting its profile fuelled by three years of ground-breaking ‘BookSeva'.InIT Solutions Pvt Ltd was honoured with the ‘ Emerging Startup of the Year 2023 Award ', followed by another at the Entrepreneurship Conclave 2023 (EC2023) earlier this month, a press release said here on Saturday.The 2011-founded InIT, whose CRM solution is tailored specifically for temple administration, won the first of the two honours on September 30 at the HSX2.0 event hosted by Headstart at SAP Labs Bangalore, it said.The second came at the October 7-8 EC2023 organised by the World Konkani Centre, Saraswath Chamber and UK & Co, it said.InIT won the ‘Emerging Startup' recognition at a competition between 1,000 startups from across the country.The company emerged in the standout selections among the 70 startups shortlisted, earning it the spotlight at the Bharath Pitchathon 2.0, it said.As for the EC2023 honour, the event recognised InIT Solutions Pvt Ltd as one of the ‘Top 5 Startups' that had excelled in the SharkTank Pitching competition.The event was held before experts such as Infosys former director Mohandas Pai and Jyothi Labs ex-CEO Ullas Kamath besides 300-plus visionary entrepreneurs, investors and corporate representatives from across India.Each of these top startups, including InIT, won a prize of Rs 5 lakh, the statement further said.Besides ‘BookSeva', InIT assists temples in streamlining their day-to-day operations by implementing an ERP (enterprise resource planning) system.Notable Kerala temple administrations associating with InIT are Guruvayur, those under Cochin Devaswom Board and Attukal in Thiruvananthapuram district.InIT Solutions, which is based at Vennala in the city, is working towards expanding its services to temple management across India, it added.KSUM is Kerala government's nodal agency established in 2006 for entrepreneurship development and incubation activities.
Article Summary: InIT Solutions Pvt Ltd was honoured with the ‘ Emerging Startup of the Year 2023 Award' The company primarily connects devotees with temples through a cost-free Customer Relationship Management Solution (CRM) The 2011-founded InIT, whose CRM solution is tailored specifically for temple administration, won the first of the two honours.

Article Title: Startup BharatAgri raises Rs 35 crore from investors
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Agritech startup BharatAgri, an advisory led e-commerce platform for farmers, on Thursday said it has raised Rs 35 crore (USD 4.3 million) from investors including Arkam Ventures.The company raised Rs 35 crore in the Series A funding round.Besides Arkam Ventures the funding round also saw participation from Capria Ventures and existing investors, India Quotient, 021 Capital , and Omnivore , BharatAgri said in a release.The funding marks Arkam Ventures' third investment in the agri-tech space."The funds will be used to scale BharatAgri's e-commerce platform into new geographies and strengthen its last-mile delivery," the statement said.BharatAgri, founded by IIT Madras Alumni Siddharth Dialani and Sai Gole, has built prediction algorithms that provide advisory customised to crops, region and climatic changes.Farmers can access this custom advisory that would help them increase farm yield, lower input costs and labour effort.Its e-commerce platform offers over 10,000 agricultural products such as fertilisers, seeds, pesticides, insecticides, farming equipment, among others and is delivered pan-India, the statement said.
Article Summary: Agritech startup BharatAgri, an advisory led e-commerce platform for farmers, on Thursday said it has raised Rs 35 crore (USD 4.3 million) from investors including Arkam Ventures. The company raised Rs35 crore in the Series A funding round. The funding round also saw participation from Capria Ventures and existing investors, India Quotient, 021 Capital, and Omnivore.
